text: The channels run shallow and almost still. Little escapes: 2 Qi seeps away each turn.
A thin current stirs the meridians. 5 Qi seeps away each turn.
The meridians flow briskly, and what is not spent begins to leak. 10 Qi seeps away each turn.
Qi presses hard against its channels. 15 Qi drains away each turn.
The vessel brims beyond what flesh can hold. 25 Qi floods away each turn.
[[b]]Qi[[/b]] flows from winning battles against non-Han factions and from piercing forbidden points on the Needle Path.
[[b]]Qi[[/b]] is spent on blessing points, seeps away through decay, and is lost when battles are lost.

Qi is the breath that moves through body and realm alike. Zhang Jin gathers it from victories over the warring houses and from needles driven into forbidden points, and spends it to open the blessed meridians of the Needle Path.
Zhang Jin husbands the hidden flow of Qi. Its currents are read only within the needle master's own court.
Your attendant will raise incense altars throughout the commandery, don the red turban of the governor's order, and lead the people in ritual music until the very air hums with gathered Qi.
Your attendant will pour out the stored breath of heaven upon the garrisons: chanting, burning incense, and laying hands upon the wounded. Qi is spent, but soldiers rise from their sickbeds.

The captives are given to the altar. Drums sound, incense thickens, and the governor's red turban bows as spilled blood is transmuted into a great draught of Qi.
The defeated are washed in incense smoke and pressed into the ranks. Each new voice added to the ritual chorus carries a little more Qi to heaven.
The captives are anointed, blessed with ritual music, and sent home to speak of the governor's mercy. Heaven repays compassion with a gentle current of Qi.

Qi is this faction's unique resource: the breath of heaven that Zhang Jin, red-turbaned governor of the south, gathers through war and ritual to drive needles along the body's meridians.
• Qi is gained from battles won and lost to non-Han foes.
• Spend Qi on the Needle Path to unlock permanent blessings.
• Forbidden points grant Qi at the price of lasting afflictions.
• Taoist rites assignments and captive rituals channel more Qi.
Winning battles against non-Han factions grants [[b]]+3 Qi[[/b]]; defeats drain [[b]]2 Qi[[/b]].
The Needle Path chart offers 20 blessing points granting permanent faction-wide boons.
Twelve forbidden points grant an infusion of Qi plus a per-turn stream, but inflict permanent debuffs.
Province assignments and post-battle captive choices provide steady Qi income.
The red turban inspires: victories against the warring houses yield Qi.
Taoist ritual music steadies the provinces and mends the wounded.
The Needle Path: 32 acupoints of blessing and forbidden power.
Battle Qi rewards fighting the rival houses rather than the Han court.
Taoist Rites assignments generate Qi; the Healing Breath spends it to replenish garrisons.

Five meridians opened, and the commandery has noticed. Farmers who once queued for the physician now queue for the governor. They bring their sick, their grain, and their sons.

Ten gates of the body stand open. The elders of the commandery ask that you perform the rite publicly, at the spring altar, where all may see the breath move.\\n\\nYour officers think it undignified. The people think it is a miracle.
The altar is thronged. Qi flows freely, and so does goodwill.

The Han Court Sends a Physician
A court physician arrives from Luoyang, ostensibly to study your method. He takes careful notes and asks careful questions.\\n\\nHe is either a student or a spy, and possibly both.
The method spreads. The court is flattered; something is lost.

He leaves with an empty scroll and a full report.

Every blessed meridian in the body stands open. The red turban is no longer a governor's affectation but a physician's sigil, and men travel from three commanderies to be touched by the needle.
The needle goes where the classics forbid. Breath floods in like water through a broken dyke — and something in you does not close again afterwards.
Three forbidden points, and your commanders have begun to talk. They have seen the tremor in your hand and the colour of your lips.\\n\\nOne of them, bravely, asks whether the governor is well.
Honesty steadies them, though the truth is not comforting.

No one asks again. No one volunteers much else, either.

Six forbidden gates stand open and will not close. You sleep badly, eat little, and hear the needles humming when there are no needles in the room.

Your own physician sets down the case of needles and will not pick it up again. He says that what you are doing is not medicine, and that he will not be the hand that finishes you.\\n\\nHe offers to purge the forbidden points instead. It would cost you dearly in gathered breath.
The tremor eases. So does the flood of Qi you had grown used to.

You do not need him. You have not needed anyone for some time.

There is no point left on the chart that the classics permit you to have opened. Breath moves through you the way wind moves through a ruined house — freely, and without resistance, because there is very little left to resist it.
A dozen points marked in cinnabar on the body chart. Your clerks have begun keeping a second ledger, tracking not grain or men but breath.

Two dozen points opened, and men have come to study under you. They sleep in the yard and copy your chart by lamplight.\\n\\nThey could be trained as physicians for the army, or sent away before they learn what the forbidden points cost.

Word of the needle master travels ahead of his banners.
